title: The Birthday Bake Sale
sum: Tessa doubles Nana's apple muffin recipe, invites an old neighbor, and sells 24 muffins at her school's 50th birthday bake sale.

cast.d: a seven-year-old second grader who loves to measure and count
cast.look: a seven-year-old girl with two curly puffs of hair, a green apron and a pencil behind her ear

cast.d: Tessa's grandmother, who bakes from an old recipe box
cast.look: a tall grandmother with short gray hair, round glasses and flour on her sleeves

cast.d: Tessa's classmate from the next desk, who has never baked before
cast.look: a seven-year-old boy with short black hair and a red striped shirt

cast.d: Nana's little brown dog, who waits for crumbs
cast.look: a small brown dog with floppy ears and a white spot on his chest

cast.d: an old neighbor in the yellow house, who was the school's first teacher
cast.look: an older woman with white hair in a bun and a big purple sweater
a young woman with long dark hair and a yellow cardigan

p: Tessa dropped her backpack in Nana Bea's kitchen. Biscuit, Nana's little brown dog, sniffed at a yellow note sticking out of the pocket.
Tessa unfolded the note and read it out loud. “Maple Street School turns 50 on Friday! Come to our Birthday Bake Sale. Please send 24 muffins. The money will buy a new maple tree for the playground.”
Nana found her old recipe card, the one with a butter spot. APPLE MUFFINS, it said across the top. The bottom line said Makes 12.
Tessa frowned at the card. “Twelve is not enough,” she said. “We need twenty-four.”
“Then we double it,” said Nana. “Double? Like a double scoop?” Tessa asked. Nana laughed. “Just like that. One scoop, then one more on top.”
Nana tapped the card. “This card is older than your mom,” she said. “So first, a practice batch. We'll bake the real ones on Thursday.”
Tessa got the butter out of the fridge. It was cold and hard, like a bar of soap. She pressed it with her thumb. Nothing.
Nana set the butter on the windowsill, right in a square of sunshine. “Give it twenty minutes,” she said. “The sun will do the work.”
While the butter waited, Tessa made a new card for Thursday. At the top she wrote Makes 24. One egg became two eggs, and one cup of buttermilk became two cups.
Next came the flour. Nana's card said 2 cups. Tessa held up two fingers, and then two more. She wrote the new number and underlined it twice.
Twenty minutes later, the butter was shiny at the edges. Tessa poked it again. This time her finger sank right in, like pressing play dough.
Nana beat the soft butter and sugar. In went the egg and the buttermilk. Tessa scooped in the flour, and a white cloud puffed up. She sneezed. Under the table, Biscuit sneezed too.
Nana stirred in a teaspoon of baking soda and the chopped apples. Tessa spooned the batter into the tray, one cup at a time.
Soon the kitchen smelled like apples. Biscuit sat by the oven and did not move. Ding! Out came the muffins, tall and golden.
Tessa and Nana each ate one, still warm. “Practice muffins don't count,” said Nana, and she took another. Tessa taped her new card to the fridge. Makes 24, it said, in big blue letters.

art.s: A girl and her grandmother in a sunny kitchen, with a block of butter on the windowsill, an old recipe card on the counter and a small brown dog sneezing under the table.

q.q: Draw the butter two times: cold from the fridge, and after it sat in the sun.
look: a hard block of butter from the fridge
soft, shiny butter on the sunny windowsill
the sun shining through the window
q.e: The warm sun made the butter soft. You showed the change!

q.q: Nana said, “Then we double it.” What does double mean here?
q.e: Double means two times as much, like a double scoop: one scoop, then one more.

q.q: Nana's card needs 2 cups of flour. How many cups does Tessa need for 24 muffins?
q.e: Two cups and two more cups make four cups.

p: On Tuesday, Ms. Lopez gave every second grader a blank card. “Invite someone from your street to our bake sale,” she said. “Pick someone who might not know about it.”
Tessa knew right away. Mrs. Bell lived in the yellow house at the end of Nana's street. Every morning she sat on her porch and waved at the kids walking to school.
Tessa wrote in her neatest letters. “Dear Mrs. Bell, please come to our Birthday Bake Sale on Friday at 2:30. We will have apple muffins. Love, Tessa.”
Omar leaned over from the next desk and read it with his finger. “Where is it?” he asked. Tessa stared at her card. She had forgotten to write where!
Her cheeks went warm. She squeezed in one more line: “On the playground, under the big maple tree.”
Then she drew a little clock in the corner. The long hand pointed straight down at the 6. The short hand sat halfway between the 2 and the 3. “Half past two,” said Omar. “Nice clock.”
After school, Nana met Tessa at the gate, and they walked home past the yellow house. Maple leaves covered the sidewalk. Crunch, crunch, crunch, went Tessa's shoes.
Tessa picked up a leaf. Half of it was green, and half was bright red. “Why is it two colors?” she asked.
Nana held the leaf up to the sky. “It's fall,” she said. “The days are getting shorter and colder, so the green fades away. Red and yellow take its place.”
Tessa hunted for the reddest leaf on the whole street. It was as big as her hand. She tucked it into the envelope, right behind the card.
Mrs. Bell was on her porch in a big purple sweater. Tessa ran up the steps and held out the envelope. Mrs. Bell put on her glasses. Out came the red leaf, and then the card.
She read every word and touched the little clock with one finger. “Maple Street School,” she said. “I haven't been there in a long, long time.”

Mrs. Bell stood the card in her front window, with the red leaf beside it. “Half past two on Friday,” she said. “I'll be there.” From the corner, Tessa looked back. The red leaf was still in the window.

art.s: A girl hands an envelope with a red maple leaf to an older woman in a purple sweater on the porch of a yellow house, with fall leaves on the sidewalk.

q.q: Draw the little clock from Tessa's invitation. Make it show half past two.
look: the long hand pointing at the 6
the short hand between the 2 and the 3
the numbers 1 to 12 around the edge
q.e: Half past two is thirty minutes after two o'clock. Your clock is ready for the sale!

q.q: Why was the maple leaf turning red?
q.a: Because it was fall, and the days were getting shorter and colder.
q.e: In fall, the green fades away from the leaves. Red and yellow take its place.

q.q: What did Tessa forget to write on her invitation at first?
q.e: Omar asked, “Where is it?” So Tessa added a line about the playground and the maple tree.

p: On Thursday, Omar came to Nana's house to bake. He sat next to Tessa at school, but he had never baked before. His dad's apron hung all the way down to his socks.

Tessa took her card off the fridge. “I read, you measure,” she said. Omar scooped four cups of flour into the big bowl, one after another. Then came sugar, butter, two eggs, buttermilk and four chopped apples.
Nana's oven was small, so it could only hold one tray at a time. Omar filled all twelve cups with batter. Nana slid the tray in and set the timer.
Twenty minutes later, Nana opened the oven door. Everyone leaned in. The muffins had not puffed up at all.
“They look like pancakes,” said Omar. He tapped one. Tap, tap. Tessa's ears went hot, because they had followed her card line by line.
Nana held Tessa's card next to her own old card. Her finger slid down the lines and stopped. “Baking soda,” she said. “It's not on your card.”
Tessa looked. Eggs, buttermilk, flour, sugar. No baking soda! She had copied the card too fast on Monday, and she had skipped a line.
Nana poured a little vinegar into a glass. “Watch this,” she said, and she dropped in a teaspoon of baking soda. Fizz! White foam climbed up the glass and spilled over the top. Biscuit barked at it.

“Baking soda needs something sour,” said Nana. “Like lemon?” Omar asked. Nana wiped up the foam. “Lemon, vinegar or buttermilk. When they mix, they make tiny bubbles. The bubbles puff up the batter, like breath in a balloon.”

Half of the batter was still in the bowl. Tessa stirred in one teaspoon of baking soda, and Omar filled the second tray. This time they watched through the oven window. The muffins rose like little hills.
Now twelve puffy muffins sat on the rack. Tessa needed twenty-four for Friday. Nana pulled her old card out of the box again. “One more batch,” she said. “We have time.”
Tessa found a red pen and fixed her own card. At the bottom she wrote 2 teaspoons baking soda, with a big star. Then they mixed one more batch, and the third tray went into the oven.
While it baked, they ate the flat muffins with strawberry jam. “Pancake muffins,” said Omar, with his mouth full. “My favorite kind.”

art.s: Two children and a grandmother stare at a tray of flat muffins while a glass of vinegar foams over on the kitchen counter and a small dog barks at it.

q.q: Tessa needed 24 muffins for Friday. She had 12 puffy ones. How many more did she need?
q.e: Twelve and twelve more make twenty-four. That's why Nana made one more batch.

q.q: Draw Omar holding a flat muffin. Add a speech bubble with what he said.
look: a speech bubble coming from his mouth
q.e: A speech bubble shows what someone says. Omar would laugh at your picture!

q.q: What made the second tray of muffins puff up?
q.e: Baking soda and sour buttermilk made tiny bubbles. The bubbles puffed up the muffins.

p: By six o'clock, twenty-four puffy muffins sat on the cooling racks. Little curls of steam rose from their tops. Tessa wanted every muffin in a bag with a ribbon, right now.
She slid the first muffin into a clear bag. Omar tied the ribbon in a big floppy bow. It looked like a tiny birthday present.
A few minutes later, the bag was cloudy. Tiny drops of water covered the inside. When Tessa opened it, the top of the muffin was wet and sticky. “It's sweating!” said Omar.
Nana held up the bag. “The muffins are still warm, so they give off steam,” she said. “The steam hits the bag and turns back into water. Wet bags make soggy muffins.”
“So we have to wait?” Tessa asked. Nana set the timer for one hour. Tessa flopped onto a chair with a groan. Biscuit flopped down on her feet.
To pass the time, they made a sign for the sale. Tessa wrote APPLE MUFINS in big green letters. Omar tipped his head to one side. “Muffins has two F's,” he said.
Tessa squeezed a tiny F in after the first one. Now the sign said MUFFINS, with one skinny F. Under that she wrote the price, 50¢. Omar drew a candle and wrote HAPPY 50TH BIRTHDAY!

“What if people don't have the right coins?” Omar asked. Nana brought out her big coin jar and tipped it over. Crash! Coins rolled everywhere, and one rolled under the fridge. They picked them up and made fifty cents in different ways.
Tessa lined up five dimes. Ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty. Omar picked up a shiny quarter. “This one is twenty-five cents,” he said. “How many of these make fifty?”
Ding! The hour was up. Tessa touched a muffin, and it felt cool, like the counter. This time the bags stayed clear.
By seven o'clock, all twenty-four muffins were in bags with ribbons. Nana set the sign on top of the box. Biscuit sat under the counter all evening. Not one crumb fell.

art.s: Two children make a sign that says APPLE MUFFINS 50¢ at a kitchen table covered in coins, next to muffins cooling on racks and a small dog lying on the floor.

q.q: Draw the sign for Tessa and Omar's muffin table. Show what they sell and the price.
look: a birthday candle or a muffin
q.e: A good sign tells people what you sell and what it costs. Yours does!

q.q: Why did the inside of the first bag get wet?
q.a: The warm muffin gave off steam, and the steam turned into water.
q.e: Warm muffins give off steam. On the bag, the steam turned back into water drops.

q.q: A muffin costs 50¢. Which coins make 50¢?
q.e: A quarter is 25¢. Twenty-five and twenty-five make fifty.

p: At half past two on Friday, the playground looked like a party. A long banner said HAPPY 50TH BIRTHDAY, MAPLE STREET! Above it all stood the old maple tree, red and gold.
Tessa and Omar had a table right under the tree. Their sign stood in front, skinny F and all. Twenty-four muffins sat in neat rows.
Ms. Lopez was their first customer. She bought two muffins and paid with a dollar bill. Omar put it in their tin as if it were made of gold.
Next came a first grader with a paper cup full of pennies. He poured them out. Clink, clink, clink! Omar made stacks of ten while Tessa counted. Ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty.
“Fifty cents,” said Tessa. The boy grinned and picked the biggest muffin. By three o'clock, only four muffins were left.
Ms. Lopez came by with the class money box. “Forty-eight dollars,” she said. “The tree costs fifty.” Tessa looked at her last four muffins.
Then a gust of wind shook the tree. Maple seeds came spinning down, round and round, like tiny helicopters. One landed right on the tin.
Omar picked it up. The seed had one thin, papery wing. He held it high and let go. It twirled all the way down to the grass. “Why does it spin?” Tessa asked.

“So it can travel,” said a voice. Mrs. Bell stood there in her purple sweater, holding Tessa's envelope with the red leaf. “The wing makes it spin, so it falls slowly. Then the wind can carry it far away.”
Tessa jumped up so fast that her chair tipped over. “You came!” Mrs. Bell patted the rough trunk. “Fifty years ago, I was the first teacher here. My class planted this tree. It was as tall as me.”
Tessa looked up at the tree. Then she looked up some more. Its top branches were higher than the school roof.
Mrs. Bell bought the last four muffins and paid with two dollar bills. Tessa turned the sign over and wrote SOLD OUT in big letters.
Omar ran the two dollars over to the class box. Ms. Lopez counted it all again, and the whole second grade cheered.
Mrs. Bell ate her muffin on the bench under the old maple. Tessa gave her the spinning seed. Mrs. Bell tucked it into the envelope, right next to the red leaf.

art.s: A school playground bake sale under a huge red and gold maple tree, with maple seeds spinning down onto a muffin table and an older woman in a purple sweater holding an envelope.

q.q: Tessa turned the sign over. What two words did she write?
q.e: Sold out means every muffin is gone. What a sale!

q.q: The class box held $48. Then Mrs. Bell's $2 went in. How much was in the box?
q.e: Forty-eight and two more make fifty. That was just enough for the new tree!

q.q: Draw a maple seed falling from the tree. Show how it moves.
look: a seed with one thin wing
lines or arrows that show it spinning
the tree above it, or the wind
q.e: The wing makes the seed spin, so it falls slowly and the wind can carry it far.

fin.q: Each muffin cost 50¢, and Tessa sold all 24. How many dollars did her muffins make?
fin.e: Two muffins make one dollar. So 24 muffins make 12 dollars.

fin.q: Which change happened because something got warm?
fin.e: The warm sun made the butter soft. The leaves turned red because the days got colder.
